content: The search strategy employed databases such as CINAHL Plus, Global Health, and POPLINE, with a broad approach to ensure comprehensive coverage. The search was restricted to studies published after the year 2000, coinciding with the registration of the WHO-focused antenatal care (ANC) trial, or after 2002, when the WHO ANC implementation guide was published. The search string for MEDLINE was customized for each database and included terms related to antenatal and perinatal care. The search was limited to studies published from 2000 to the present. The search strategy for antenatal care was adapted from Cochrane reviews on ANC, and country-specific keywords were derived from the MEDLINE lowand middle-income country (LMIC) filter. Reference lists of all relevant studies and bibliographies of systematic reviews identified during the search were examined. Reports were required to be available in English or the primary language spoken in the selected country cases. For unpublished literature, information was gathered from ministry of health documents (via web searches and local contacts), online databases, and websites of organizations involved in maternal and child health, as well as donor and implementation partner websites. Web searches were conducted using keywords such as antenatal care and the country name. Formal appraisal of study quality was not conducted due to the anticipated variability in the quality, scope, and format of the available literature. Instead, a narrative description of the included studies and reports was undertaken. Primary data collection was conducted through key informant interviews to address gaps in published and online information, particularly for cases with limited adoption or unsuccessful implementation of the WHO-focused ANC model (FANC). Up to five stakeholders were identified for each country case, using purposive sampling to ensure maximum variation and representation of diverse experiences with the 2016 WHO ANC model. Stakeholders included policymakers, managers, donors, researchers, private sector representatives, healthcare providers, and service users. Interviews were conducted face-to-face or via phone, with detailed notes taken during the discussions. Interviews were conducted in English or the primary language of the country, depending on the interviewer's background. The interview topic guide was informed by existing data (or lack thereof) for each case. The interviews were designed to be open and flexible, allowing participants to discuss their experiences and perceptions of the FANC model in detail. For each country case, a short profile was developed, including indicators such as mortality rates, resource availability (human and capital), ANC coverage and content, and other relevant metrics on access, equity, and development. Where possible, time trends for key variables were provided. These indicators were compiled from publicly available datasets, including those from WHO and the World Bank. The technical team also considered indirect evidence for health systems interventions to supplement existing direct evidence. This was particularly relevant for three priority questions: (1) Should group ANC be recommended as an alternative to standard ANC? (2) What interventions should be recommended to communicate with and support pregnant women, their partners, and communities about maintaining health during pregnancy and using ANC services? (3) Should pregnant women carry their own ANC case notes? Indirect evidence was included if it had been part of a systematic review published within the last five years, was relevant to the ANC guideline question, and addressed agreed-upon outcomes. For questions 1 and 3, the team initially searched PDQ Evidence for relevant reviews, using terms such as group care and patient-held notes. Reviews published within the last five years were screened for relevance. For question 2, reviews conducted by the Cochrane Consumers and Communication Review Group were screened for indirect evidence. Each review meeting the inclusion criteria was summarized, and its relevance was discussed within the technical team. The technical team aimed to maximize the identification of relevant indirect evidence within the available time. Search terms were generated and refined to focus on the priority questions, and searches were conducted for reviews published in the last five years. Titles and abstracts were screened to identify potentially relevant reviews, and the analysis and search functions in PDQ Evidence were used to identify direct and indirect evidence.
